content: The Royal Victoria Hospital, commonly referred to as The Royal or RVH, is a prominent medical facility located in Belfast, Northern Ireland. It provides over 20% of the acute care beds in Northern Ireland and treats approximately half a million patients annually. The hospital is currently undergoing a £74 million refurbishment, which includes an extension to the Royal Belfast Hospital for Sick Children, the addition of new wards in the main hospital, a new Accident & Emergency department, and a new maternity unit. The hospital is situated just a few minutes from Belfast's City Centre in the western part of the city. Completed in 1906, the Royal Victoria Hospital is a landmark in architectural and engineering history, as it is considered the first air-conditioned building in the world. The air conditioning system was developed by Belfast's Sirocco Works factory, which was a pioneer in this technology. Dr. Frank Pantridge, often referred to as the father of emergency medicine, served as a cardiac consultant at the hospital for over three decades. During his tenure, he invented the portable defibrillator, a groundbreaking device that revolutionized emergency medicine by enabling paramedics to provide early treatment to patients experiencing cardiac arrest. Carmel Hanna, a Social Democratic and Labour Party (SDLP) politician, worked as a nurse at the hospital. David Ervine, a Progressive Unionist Party (PUP) politician, was admitted to the hospital on January 7, 2007, and passed away there the following day. During the Northern Ireland Troubles, the Royal Victoria Hospital gained international recognition for its expertise in treating gunshot wounds, particularly injuries to the knee. This expertise was developed due to the high number of punishment shootings targeting the kneecaps, which were a common occurrence during the conflict. The surgeons at the hospital became renowned for their skill in managing and treating such injuries.
